Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

derivations.claim: Applying the three tensor products in [F1] to the ordered basis $(00,01,10,11)$ gives the matrix with outer diagonal entries $1,1$, middle block $\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and all other entries zero.

derivations.claim: Write $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}u&z\\\overline z&1-u\end{pmatrix}$, where $u\in\mathbb R$ because $\rho$ is Hermitian and the lower diagonal entry is fixed by $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Set $a_x=2\operatorname{Re}z$, $a_y=-2\operatorname{Im}z$, and $a_z=2u-1$. Direct substitution of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\rho=\tfrac12(I+a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z)$. Direct multiplication gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)=a_j$ for each $j$, so the entries of $\rho$ force uniqueness and each coefficient is real.

The displayed matrix $A:=a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a_z&a_x-ia_y\\a_x+ia_y&-a_z\end{pmatrix}$. Expanding its $2\times2$ determinant gives $\det(\lambda I-A)=\lambda^2-a_x^2-a_y^2-a_z^2=\lambda^2-|a|^2$. Use the ordered tensor-product basis $(e_0\otimes e_0,e_0\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_0,e_1\otimes e_1)$ of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$. Its inner product is the linear-first product inner product, specified on elementary tensors by $\langle u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'\rangle=\langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly. For two $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$, their tensor product acts by $(A\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv$ and is extended linearly.

Write $I_2:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for the identity on $\mathbb C^2$, use $I:=I_2$ when its domain is clear, and set $I_4:=I_2\otimes I_2$. Define the everywhere-defined matrices

$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Define the dimensionless exchange matrix

$$C:=\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x+\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y+\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z.$$

For a finite matrix $A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ denotes the sum of its diagonal entries in the displayed basis. Each $\sigma_j$ and $C$ is Hermitian and has full finite-dimensional domain.

For $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], the singlet vector $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplet vectors $e_0\otimes e_0$, $(e_0\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$, and $e_1\otimes e_1$ have eigenvalue $1$. $$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n\qquad(x\in N_r(c)).$$

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: In the ordered basis $e_0e_0,e_0e_1,e_1e_0,e_1e_1$, the field operator $\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z$ has eigenvalues $2,0,0,-2$. The middle two basis vectors combine into the singlet and the $m=0$ triplet of [F2]; both have field eigenvalue $0$. The outer vectors are the $m=+1$ and $m=-1$ triplets, with field eigenvalues $2$ and $-2$. Since $H_{J,h}$ is a linear combination of these commuting matrices, the singlet energy is $-3J$ and the triplet energies are $J-2h,J,J+2h$.

The canonical trace is the sum of the four positive weights associated with step 1.1. It is therefore finite and positive, and the adopted preparation [A1] gives the displayed partition function. At $h=0$ and $J>0$, setting $x=\beta J$ identifies its normalized state with $\rho_x$ in [F3], so that theorem gives the exact separability and entanglement alternatives, including the equality case.

Fix $J,h$ and let $E_{\min}$ be the least of the four energies from step 1.1, with multiplicity $g$. Write the other energies as $E_{\min}+\Delta_i$ with $\Delta_i>0$. After factoring out $e^{-\beta E_{\min}}$, the denominator is $D_\beta=g+\sum_i e^{-\beta\Delta_i}\to g$ and $1\le D_\beta\le4$. The Gibbs probability of each ground vector is $1/D_\beta$, so the total ground entropy tends to $-k_Bg(1/g)\log(1/g)=k_B\log g$. For an excited vector, $p_i=e^{-\beta\Delta_i}/D_\beta$ and $-p_i\log p_i=p_i(\beta\Delta_i+\log D_\beta)\le e^{-\beta\Delta_i}(\beta\Delta_i+\log4)$; this tends to zero by [F9], so the finite sum of excited entropy terms vanishes. At $h=0$, the triplet is the three-dimensional ground space for $J<0$, all four levels coincide for $J=0$, and the singlet is the unique ground state for $J>0$, giving the stated limits.

Fix $J,h$ and any $\beta_0>0$. By [F8], $\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)$; by [F7], $\exp'(y_0)=\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)\ne0$. The real analytic inverse theorem gives a local analytic inverse to $\exp$ near $Z(\beta_0)$, and [F8] identifies that inverse with $\log$. The composition clause of [F6] now makes $\log Z$ real analytic near $\beta_0$. Since $\beta_0$ was arbitrary, $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is real analytic for every $\beta>0$: the identity and constant functions have local polynomial series, so the quotient clause of [F6] makes $\beta\mapsto\beta^{-1}$ analytic on this domain. Thus the finite-volume free energy has no singularity at the entanglement threshold.

For $J>0$, the lowest triplet energy is $J-2|h|$. It equals the singlet energy $-3J$ exactly at $|h|=2J$. The two energy levels can cross as parameters vary, but step 2.1 is a strictly positive finite sum of exponentials at every $\beta>0$, so this zero-temperature ground-space crossing creates no finite-temperature singularity.

For a declared nonrelativistic quantum model, adopt a complex Hilbert space, positive trace-one states, and Born probabilities for its specified measurements. Specify the one-particle modes, Hamiltonian and interactions. When the modeled particles are assigned bosonic or fermionic statistics, choose the symmetric or antisymmetric sector, respectively, as an independent physical assumption. This selection is not derived from the Fock construction or a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

For a canonical preparation at inverse temperature $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}>0$, adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ on the declared fixed-particle-number sector only when $0<Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation with chemical potential $\mu$, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta(H-\mu N)}$ only when the corresponding trace is finite and positive, as explicitly checked for the diagonal Fock model in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Fixed-number and grand-canonical preparations are distinct assumptions; in general the latter has independent mode occupations while conditioning on fixed total number couples them.

The assignments of $U=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)$, $S=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$ and thermodynamic potentials are model definitions where their traces exist. An identification with measured macroscopic thermodynamic quantities requires a separate physical bridge. No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
in the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

Specify the one-particle modes, Hamiltonian and interactions. When the modeled particles are assigned bosonic or fermionic statistics, choose the symmetric or antisymmetric sector, respectively, as an independent physical assumption. This selection is not derived from the Fock construction or a nonrelativistic spin-statistics theorem.

For a canonical preparation at inverse temperature $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}>0$, adopt $\rho=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ on the declared fixed-particle-number sector only when $0<Z=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}<\infty$. For a grand-canonical preparation with chemical potential $\mu$, adopt $\rho=\Xi^{-1}e^{-\beta(H-\mu N)}$ only when the corresponding trace is finite and positive, as explicitly checked for the diagonal Fock model in [[lem-qsm-models-diagonal-occupation-trace]]. Fixed-number and grand-canonical preparations are distinct assumptions; in general the latter has independent mode occupations while conditioning on fixed total number couples them.

No thermalization mechanism, empirical value, or law for a particular material is postulated here.

Fix $n\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. A real analytic germ at $a$ is an equivalence class of real functions agreeing on a neighborhood of $a$, represented on some polydisc $|x_i-a_i|<r_i$, $r_i>0$, by an absolutely convergent series $f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n}c_\alpha(x-a)^\alpha$ with real coefficients. Here $0\in\mathbb N$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $c_\alpha=D^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$. A vector germ has a finite positive number of such components, with a common polydisc obtained by taking coordinatewise minima of their radii.

The multi-index convention and absolute convergence are those of [[def-multivariable-power-series]]; for $n=1$ this agrees with [[def-real-analytic-function]]. The same coefficients define the complexification. Indeed choose a positive real polyradius $s<r$; absolute convergence at $a+s$ bounds $|c_\alpha|s^\alpha$ uniformly. [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]] therefore gives a holomorphic sum on the complex $s$-polydisc and the displayed derivative formula. Restriction to the real slice recovers $f$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$, a polyradius $r$, a real $M\ge0$ and
coefficients $c:\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ with

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}\qquad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha.$$

Then:

1. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
   $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
   $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$, so its sum $g$ is defined on
   $\Delta_r(a)$;
2. $g$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_r(a)$, with
   $$Dg(z)h=\sum_{k<m}b_k(z)h_k,\qquad b_k(z)=\sum_{\alpha}\alpha_k\,c_\alpha(z-a)^{\alpha-e_k},$$
   the $k$th series running over the multi-indices with $\alpha_k\ge1$ and
   converging absolutely on $\Delta_r(a)$; equivalently
   $\partial_{z_k}g=b_k$;
3. for every $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the derived coefficients
   $\alpha_kc_\alpha$, re-indexed as a power series, obey a bound of the same
   shape on the polyradius $\theta r$, so the differentiation may be iterated;
   and every iterated complex partial derivative
   $\partial^\beta_zg:=\partial_{z_0}^{\beta_0}\cdots\partial_{z_{m-1}}^{\beta_{m-1}}g$
   exists on $\Delta_r(a)$ with
   $$\partial^\beta_zg(a)=\beta!\,c_\beta .$$

Every absolutely convergent complex series converges, and every rearrangement has the same sum. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]], [[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]].

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: The one-mode case of [F1] identifies the number basis with the standard basis of $\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$, whose finite-support span is dense. For any real diagonal multiplier with entries $\lambda_n$, testing the adjoint identity on each basis vector forces the adjoint image to have coordinates $\lambda_nc_n$, so its adjoint domain is contained in $\{c:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. Conversely, on that weighted domain [F11] makes the pairing bounded and identifies the adjoint action with the same multiplier. Thus its maximal diagonal domain is self-adjoint. Applying this calculation to $E_B(n)$, $n$, and $K_B(n)$ establishes the three domains in the Statement.

Consecutive Bose grand energies on the number basis [F1] satisfy $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=\epsilon-\mu+Un$, a strictly increasing affine sequence in $n$. It is positive at every $n\ge0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, so $0$ uniquely minimizes. For $r\ge1$, it is negative through $n=r-1$ and positive from $n=r$ exactly when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$, so $r$ uniquely minimizes. At $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increment at $n=r$ is zero while all earlier increments are negative and all later increments positive; exactly $r,r+1$ minimize.

The four Fermi basis states have grand energies $0$, $\epsilon-\mu-h$, $\epsilon-\mu+h$, and $2(\epsilon-\mu)+U$, respectively. Summing their four positive weights gives the displayed $\Xi_F$, and summing $n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow$ or $n_\uparrow n_\downarrow$ against those weights gives the stated mean and double-occupation probability. The state is well-defined because this is a finite positive sum, as required by [A1] and [F3].

Put $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$. Completing the square gives $K_B(n)=\frac U4n^2+\frac U4(n+2a/U)^2-a^2/U\ge\frac U4n^2-a^2/U$. For $n\ge1$, $n^2\ge n$, so $e^{-\beta K_B(n)}\le e^{\beta a^2/U}q^n$ with $q=e^{-\beta U/4}$. Since $\beta U/4>0$, [F5] gives $0<q<1$, and [F6] makes the geometric upper bound summable. The $n=0$ term is $1$, so $0<\Xi_B<\infty$ and [A1], [F3] give a well-defined normalized grand state. The free-mode product trace formula in [F2] is not used.

In a strict interval with unique minimizer $r$, let $\delta$ be the smaller positive adjacent energy gap from $r$ (use only the upward gap when $r=0$). For $n>r$, the gap is a sum of increments from step 1.2, each at least the upward gap at $r$; for $n<r$, it is a sum of reversed increments, each at least the downward gap from $r-1$. Hence $K_B(n)-K_B(r)\ge\delta|n-r|$. The total relative excited weight is therefore at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=2e^{-\beta\delta}/(1-e^{-\beta\delta})$, which tends to zero. At a boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increments are $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=U(n-r)$, so exactly $r,r+1$ minimize. To the right, $K_B(r+1+\ell)-K_B(r+1)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$; to the left, $K_B(r-\ell)-K_B(r)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$ whenever $r\ge\ell$. Thus the total relative excited weight is at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta U\ell}=2e^{-\beta U}/(1-e^{-\beta U})$. The normalized Gibbs probabilities from [F3] therefore concentrate on the unique number state in a strict interval, or tend to $1/2,1/2$ on the adjacent pair at a boundary.

Fix $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ with $\beta_0>0$, put $u=\beta-\beta_0$, $v=\mu-\mu_0$, $a_0=\epsilon-\mu_0-U/2$, and $K_n^0=Un^2/2+a_0n$. Then $-\beta K_B(n;\mu)=-\beta_0K_n^0-uK_n^0+\beta_0vn+uvn$, so [F5] expands each summand as $e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}e^{-uK_n^0}e^{\beta_0vn}e^{uvn}$. On radii $r_\beta=\beta_0/2$ and any fixed $r_\mu>0$, the sum of the absolute values of all terms of these three exponential power series, over all $n$, is bounded by $\sum_{n\ge0}\exp(-\beta_0K_n^0+r_\beta|K_n^0|+\beta_0r_\mu n+r_\beta r_\mu n)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $K_n^0\ge0$ and $|K_n^0|\le Un^2/2+|a_0|n$, so the exponent is at most $-\beta_0Un^2/4+Cn$ for a finite constant $C$. Increasing the cutoff so $Cn\le\beta_0Un^2/8$ leaves a tail bounded by $e^{-\beta_0Un/8}$, whose series converges by [F5]–[F6]; the finitely many initial terms are finite. Thus the total absolute coefficient sum is finite. Grouping $r+t=p$ and $s+t=q$ gives $c_{pq}=\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}\sum_{t=0}^{\min(p,q)}\frac{(-K_n^0)^{p-t}(\beta_0n)^{q-t}n^t}{(p-t)!(q-t)!t!}$. The absolute bound and [F7] justify these coefficient sums and rearrangement, and give $\sum_{p,q}|c_{pq}|r_\beta^p r_\mu^q<\infty$, hence $|c_{pq}|\le M r_\beta^{-p}r_\mu^{-q}$ for some finite $M$. Applying the multivariable power-series theorem [F7] gives a holomorphic sum on the complex polydisc; its real restriction is the absolutely convergent germ in [F4]. Since $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ was arbitrary, $\Xi_B$ is jointly real analytic on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$.

Fix $\beta>0$ and let $\mu$ range over a compact interval. The quantity $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$ is then bounded, so the square bound in step 2.1 gives $e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C e^{-\beta U n^2/4}$ for a constant $C$ uniform on that interval. Put $q=e^{-\beta U/8}\in(0,1)$. Since $n^2\ge n$, $(1+n^2)e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C(1+n^2)q^{2n}$. By [F9], $(1+n^2)q^n$ is bounded, so the right side is at most $C'q^n$, a summable geometric envelope. Apply [F8] on $\mathbb N_0$ with the counting measure [A2], weight $w(n)=e^{-\beta E_B(n)}$, observable $X(n)=n$, and natural parameter $\theta=\beta\mu$. Its hypotheses hold by this compact envelope and step 2.1; it gives $\partial_\theta\mathbb E(N_B)=\operatorname{Var}(N_B)$. The chain rule [F12] yields the displayed response, while the normalized weights give the expectation formula.

Let $g=1$ in a strict interval and $g=2$ at a boundary, and shift all energies by their minimum so the ground energy is zero. The diagonal entropy from [F3] is $S_B/k_B=\log D_\beta+\beta\sum_{n\ge0}p_nK_B(n)$, where $D_\beta=g+R_\beta$ and $R_\beta$ is the total relative excited weight from step 2.2. Thus $D_\beta\to g$ by step 2.2 and $\log D_\beta\to\log g$ by continuity [F10]. In either case, for each distance $\ell\ge1$ there are at most two excited states; their lower gaps are $\delta\ell$ by step 2.2 and their upper gaps are $C(1+\ell^2)$ because $K_B(n)$ is quadratic in $n$. Here $C$ is fixed and $\delta=U$ at a boundary. For $\beta\ge1$, [F9] makes $(1+\ell^2)e^{-\delta\ell/2}$ bounded; splitting $e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}$ therefore bounds $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}(1+\ell^2)e^{-\beta\delta\ell}$ by a constant times $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}=\beta q_\beta/(1-q_\beta)$, where $q_\beta=e^{-\beta\delta/2}$. This tends to zero by [F5], [F6], and [F9]. Consequently the excited contribution to the entropy vanishes, while the normalized ground weights contribute $0$ for $g=1$ and $\log2$ for $g=2$.

The normalized means are $\langle n_\uparrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$ and $\langle n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\downarrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$, while $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle=w_2/\Xi_F$. Subtracting the product of the means yields $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=(w_2-w_\uparrow w_\downarrow)/\Xi_F^2$. Since $w_\uparrow w_\downarrow=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}$ and $w_2=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}e^{-\beta U}$, this is the displayed formula; $U\ge0$ makes it nonpositive, with equality exactly at $U=0$.

**Periodic commuting Ising model.** For $N\ge2$, let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ and let $Z_i$ act as $\sigma_z$ on tensor factor $i$ and as identity on the others. With periodic indexing $Z_{N+1}=Z_1$, count exactly the $N$ indexed bonds, so $N=2$ has two bonds. For real energies $J,h$ and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt
$$H_N^{\mathrm q}=-J\sum_{i=1}^N Z_iZ_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i.$$
In the product eigenbasis $|s_1,\ldots,s_N\rangle$, $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, its energy equals $H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)=-J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$. Thus the quantum Gibbs density is diagonal in this basis, and its partition function and diagonal probabilities agree exactly with the specified classical finite ring. In particular, when $J\ge0$ and $h=0$, its $\sigma_z$ correlations are those of [[pthm-csm-ising-ring-correlation]]. For all real $J,h$ and $\beta>0$, define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$ and $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and put
$$\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}.$$
Then $N^{-1}\log Z_N^{\mathrm q}\to\log\lambda_+$, with every fixed finite order of derivatives converging locally uniformly on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$. This is the exact commuting one-dimensional model, not a theorem for noncommuting interactions.

**Global three-sector countermodel.** For $N\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$ joules, let $\mathcal K_N=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C\oplus(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes 2N}$ with its orthogonal direct-sum inner product, and write $I_{4^N}$ for the identity on the final $4^N$-dimensional summand. Let $|A\rangle,|B\rangle$ be the standard unit vectors in the first and second summands, and let $|s\rangle$ range over the standard product basis in the final summand. Define $H_N^{\mathrm g}=0\oplus N\epsilon\oplus2N\epsilon I_{4^N}$, so the basis energies are $E(A)=0$, $E(B)=N\epsilon$, and $E(s)=2N\epsilon$. For $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define the spectral-shell basis subset $S_{N,\Delta}:=\{v:|E(v)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and its uniform state $\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}:=|S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}\sum_{v\in S_{N,\Delta}}|v\rangle\langle v|$. For $\beta>0$ this finite quantum model has
$$Z_N^{\mathrm g}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}.$$
For every real $\beta$ as an algebraic finite-weight extension, the normalized exponential-tilt weight of the one-dimensional middle sector is at most $(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$; the shell state above assigns that sector probability $1$. The term “probability” here is the trace of the state against the middle-sector projection $|B\rangle\langle B|$. Also
$$\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}\longrightarrow\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\},\qquad 0\le\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}-\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}\le\frac{\log3}{N}.$$
The limiting function has a corner at $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$; the canonical mean energy per member tends to $2\epsilon$ from below, $0$ from above, and $\epsilon$ at $\beta_c$. Every finite-$N$ partition sum is analytic. This global, size-dependent family is not a product of one fixed finite one-site alphabet and makes no claim about local or short-range matter.

derivations.claim: At $N=2$ and $\beta=\beta_c$, $e^{-\beta N\epsilon}=e^{-2\log2}=1/4$ and $4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}=16e^{-4\log2}=1$. Hence $Z_2=9/4$ and the middle-sector Gibbs probability is $(1/4)/(9/4)=1/9$. The finite partition is a sum of positive exponentials, so it is analytic at this parameter.

Since $2\epsilon$ is the distance from the middle energy to either outer energy at $N=2$, every shell with $0\le\Delta<2\epsilon$ selects exactly the one-dimensional middle sector and gives it uniform probability $1$. Thus the two specified finite preparations disagree on this observable, while the analytic finite sum and limiting cusp remain distinct claims.

Let $e_0,e_1$ and $\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z,C$ be as in [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], with $\sigma_z e_0=e_0$ and $\sigma_z e_1=-e_1$. By [[lem-qsm-pauli-dimer-spectrum]], the normalized singlet $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ has $C$-eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplets have eigenvalue $1$. Adopt the two-spin Hamiltonian
$$H_{J,h}:=JC-h(\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z)$$
on $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$, where $J,h\in\mathbb R$ are energies in joules. For inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, use the canonical Gibbs preparation only after normalizing its finite trace. Its singlet energy is $-3J$; its triplet energies are $J-2h$, $J$, and $J+2h$. Here $\cosh y:=(e^y+e^{-y})/2$.
$$Z(\beta,J,h)=e^{3\beta J}+e^{-\beta J}\bigl(1+2\cosh(2\beta h)\bigr)>0.$$
At $h=0$ and $J>0$, the Gibbs density matrix is entangled exactly when $\beta J>(\log3)/4$, and is separable at and below equality. This exact threshold is a finite-state quantum-model conclusion. For every fixed $J,h$, $Z$ and the free energy $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ are real analytic for $\beta>0$; the entanglement threshold is not a finite-temperature thermodynamic singularity. At zero field the entropy tends to $0$ as $\beta\to\infty$ for $J>0$, to $k_B\log3$ for $J<0$, and to $k_B\log4$ for $J=0$. For $J>0$, a nonzero field makes the singlet and the field-aligned triplet cross at $|h|=2J$ at zero temperature; this ground-space crossing does not make $Z$ singular at finite positive temperature.

**Repulsive single-mode Bose site.** Let $\mathcal H_B=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n\rangle$, supplied by the one-mode specialization of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]]. Put $E_B(n):=\epsilon n+\frac U2n(n-1)$, where $\epsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $U>0$ are in joules. Define $H_B$ and $N_B$ as real diagonal multipliers $H_B|n\rangle=E_B(n)|n\rangle$ and $N_B|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$ on their maximal domains
$$D(H_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}E_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(N_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, define $K_B$ directly as the real diagonal multiplier with eigenvalues
$$K_B(n):=E_B(n)-\mu n=\frac U2n^2+\left(\epsilon-\mu-\frac U2\right)n$$
on the exact maximal domain $D(K_B)=\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}K_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. These diagonal multipliers are self-adjoint on their displayed domains. The grand partition sum
$$\Xi_B(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$$
is finite and positive for every such $(\beta,\mu)$. It is jointly real analytic locally on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, meaning it has an absolutely convergent power-series representation in the two real parameters near every point. Its normalized diagonal Gibbs state has weights $p_n=\Xi_B^{-1}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$ and
$$\langle N_B\rangle=\Xi_B^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}n e^{-\beta K_B(n)},\qquad \partial_\mu\langle N_B\rangle=\beta\,\operatorname{Var}(N_B).$$
In the zero-temperature limit $\beta\to\infty$, the unique minimizing occupation is $0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, and is $r\ge1$ when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$. At each boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$, exactly the adjacent occupations $r,r+1$ minimize $K_B$; their probabilities tend to $1/2$ each and the model entropy $S=-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho_B\log\rho_B)$ from [[post-qsm-models-statistics-and-preparation]] tends to $k_B\log2$. In a strict interval, the unique minimizing number state has probability tending to one and entropy tending to zero.

**Two-mode Fermi Hubbard atom.** On $\mathcal H_F=\mathbb C^4$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, $n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\in\{0,1\}$, define $n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$ and $n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, and adopt
$$H_F=\epsilon(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)+U n_\uparrow n_\downarrow-h(n_\uparrow-n_\downarrow),$$
where $\epsilon,\mu,U,h$ are in joules, $U\ge0$, and $\beta>0$. With $K_F=H_F-\mu(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)$, its grand partition function and weights are
$$\Xi_F=1+w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+w_2,\quad w_\uparrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu-h)},\quad w_\downarrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu+h)},\quad w_2=e^{-\beta(2(\epsilon-\mu)+U)}.$$
Thus $\langle n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+2w_2)/\Xi_F$, the double-occupation probability $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle$ is $w_2/\Xi_F$, and, with $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow):=\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle-\langle n_\uparrow\rangle\langle n_\downarrow\rangle$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=\frac{e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}(e^{-\beta U}-1)}{\Xi_F^2}\le0.$$
The covariance is zero at $U=0$ and strictly negative at $U>0$. These are exact conditional model calculations, not claims about measured atoms.
